clinicalClaims.text: Historical scores describe severity and cohort outcomes, not individual recovery ceilings. In critically ill adults with ischemic stroke, admission NIHSS or ASTRAL alone is not reliable for poor-outcome counseling. The ICH Score can provide a general framework for communication, but no score should be the sole basis for an individual prognosis or for withholding reperfusion, decompression or life-sustaining treatment.
clinicalClaims.population: Interpret each score in its original population and outcome horizon. Historical cohort outcomes are not an individual prognosis.
clinicalClaims.limits: Do not combine score definitions or outcome models. Preserve missing-input states and model-specific uncertainty.
clinicalClaims.reviewScope: Recorded review covers the cited ICH and AIS guidance, not validation of every prognostic model. The AIS source retains an unresolved body/table evidence-grade discrepancy for ASTRAL.

guidelines.title: AHA/ASA Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke 2026

correctedBy.note: Recovered correction items 12, 13, 22, 23 and 24 support the five linked recommendation repairs, including PES Class IIb. The complete seven-page notice was not recovered: portions of items 8, 11 and 25, references 19/34 and final page e467 remain incomplete. This is a partial correction review, not certification of the full current edition.

recommendations.text: Measurement and documentation of baseline stroke severity (e.g., NIHSS score) in all acute stroke patients is recommended to enable sufficiently accurate and reliable risk adjustment models for comparing facility performance.

Emergent brain imaging with NCCT or MRI is recommended on initial evaluation of suspected AIS to assess ischemic burden (e.g., ASPECTS) and exclude intracranial hemorrhage before initiating reperfusion interventions.

Facilities caring for suspected AIS patients are recommended to establish process improvement protocols so emergent brain imaging can be performed as rapidly as possible (e.g., within 25 minutes) to facilitate timely reperfusion interventions.
In patients with suspected AIS and LVO, emergent vascular imaging with CTA and/or CTP is recommended not to be delayed to obtain serum creatinine.

In pediatric patients with suspected AIS, emergent brain and vascular imaging with MRI/MRA of the cervical and intracranial vessels is reasonable to identify LVO and differentiate arterial ischemic stroke from hemorrhagic stroke or stroke mimics.
In pediatric patients with suspected AIS, emergent CT/CTA of the cervical and intracranial vessels is reasonable when MRI/MRA is not immediately available (within 25 minutes) to identify LVO.

In patients with suspected AIS who awaken with symptoms or have unknown time of onset beyond 4.5 hours from last known well but are otherwise eligible for thrombolysis, MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch selection can be useful to determine eligibility for extended-window IVT.

In patients with suspected AIS who awaken with symptoms or have unknown time of onset 4.5 to 24 hours from last known well, CTP or MR DWI-PWI selection with automated postprocessing software can be useful to determine eligibility for extended-window IVT.

In patients with suspected AIS and LVO presenting within 24 hours of last known well, emergent brain and vascular imaging (CT/CTA or MRI/MRA) of the cervical and intracranial vessels is recommended to be performed as rapidly as possible for EVT selection and treatment planning.

In patients with suspected AIS and LVO presenting 6 to 24 hours from last known well, adjunctive CTP, MRI (DWI-FLAIR mismatch), or MR DWI-PWI with automated postprocessing software can be useful in EVT evaluation if immediately available.

In patients with suspected AIS and LVO identified by prefacility assessment with a validated stroke severity scale (e.g., RACE >4) who are EVT-eligible, direct triage to the angiography suite for flat-panel head CT may be considered to reduce time to intervention and improve functional outcomes compared with conventional imaging workflow.
recommendations.currentEvidenceNote: Newer evidence reviewed 2026-09-26: DIRECT ANGIO (Lancet Neurology, 2026), a French multicenter RCT published after this guideline, randomly assigned 115 patients aged 85 years or younger who were admitted directly to an endovascular-capable center within 5 hours of onset with a severe deficit suggestive of LVO (selected by neurologist examination on arrival, not a prehospital scale) to direct transfer to the angiography suite for cone-beam CT and angiography or to conventional imaging first. It was stopped early for safety. Symptomatic ICH was higher with direct transfer (5/34 vs 0/42; adjusted OR 11.0, 95% CI 1.28-1406), with no evidence of functional benefit (mRS 0-2 at 90 days 36% vs 42%; adjusted OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.32-1.69). The small sample limits precision. This IIb recommendation predates the trial, so read its stated functional-outcome benefit with caution.

recommendations.text: In emergently transferred patients with suspected AIS due to LVO who are EVT-eligible, direct triage to the angiography suite may be considered without repeat brain imaging on arrival at the thrombectomy center, unless there is clinical change or transfer delay.
Baseline ECG assessment is recommended in patients with suspected acute stroke but is not recommended to delay initiation of IVT or EVT.
Baseline troponin measurement is recommended in patients with suspected acute stroke but is not recommended to delay initiation of IVT or EVT.
In patients who undergo EVT, it is reasonable to maintain BP at or below 180/105 mmHg during and for 24 hours after the procedure.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation LVO who have been successfully recanalized by EVT (mTICI 2b, 2c, or 3) without other indications for specific BP targets, intensive SBP reduction to below 140 mmHg for the first 72 hours is harmful and not recommended.
In AIS patients with hyperthermia, targeting normothermia (including nurse-initiated fever management protocols) is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.
In AIS patients with hyperthermia, identifying and treating the source of fever (such as infection) is recommended to avoid complications.
In AIS patients who are normothermic, induced hypothermia or prophylactic fever prevention is not recommended as it does not improve outcomes.
In AIS patients, hypoglycemia (blood glucose below 60 mg/dL) is recommended to be treated to avoid complications.
In AIS patients, it is reasonable to treat persistent hyperglycemia to achieve blood glucose levels of 140-180 mg/dL with close monitoring to prevent worse functional outcomes.
In inpatient AIS patients with hyperglycemia, IV insulin targeting blood glucose of 80-130 mg/dL is not recommended as it does not improve 3-month functional outcomes.
In adult AIS patients with disabling deficits (regardless of NIHSS score) who are eligible for IVT, faster treatment is recommended as it improves functional outcomes.

In adult AIS patients eligible for IVT within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, treatment is recommended to be initiated as quickly as possible while ensuring safe administration, avoiding potential delays from additional multimodal neuroimaging (CTA/MRA, CT/MR perfusion).

Healthcare professionals are recommended to be prepared to treat potential emergent adverse effects of IVT, including bleeding complications and angioedema (which may cause partial airway obstruction), to reduce poor clinical outcomes.

For AIS patients eligible for IVT, it is recommended that healthcare professionals discuss potential risks and benefits with competent patients and/or available patient representatives (when feasible) to ensure shared decision-making.

Blood glucose levels are recommended to be determined before IVT initiation in suspected ischemic stroke patients to assess and urgently treat severe hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, which may mimic acute stroke presentations.

In suspected ischemic stroke patients with severe hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, if disabling stroke symptoms persist despite correction to normoglycemia, IVT administration is recommended to improve functional outcomes.

In AIS patients otherwise eligible for IVT who have early ischemic change of mild to moderate extent (other than frank hypodensity attributable to the clinical presentation) on initial brain imaging, IVT is recommended to improve functional outcome.

In eligible adult AIS patients presenting with mild, non-disabling stroke deficits (e.g., isolated sensory syndrome) within 4.5 hours of symptom onset or last known well, IVT is not recommended as it has not shown superiority over dual antiplatelet treatment for improving functional outcomes.

In suspected AIS patients taking single or dual antiplatelet therapy who are otherwise eligible for IVT, IVT is recommended to improve functional outcomes despite an increased risk of sICH compared with no antiplatelet therapy.

In AIS patients within 4.5 hours of last known well who are eligible for IVT, it is reasonable not to delay IVT while waiting for hematologic or coagulation testing if there is no reason to suspect an abnormal result.
In AIS patients eligible for IVT within 4.5 hours of symptom onset with unknown cerebral microbleed (CMB) burden, IVT is recommended to be administered without first obtaining MRI to exclude CMBs.

In AIS patients within 4.5 hours of last known well who are eligible for IVT, administration of IVT is reasonable to achieve better functional outcomes if a small number of CMBs (e.g., 1-10) was demonstrated on MRI.

In AIS patients within 4.5 hours of last known well who are eligible for IVT and previously had a high burden of CMBs (e.g., >10) on MRI, the usefulness of IVT is uncertain as it may be associated with increased sICH risk.

In pediatric patients aged 28 days to 18 years with confirmed AIS presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset with disabling deficits, IVT with alteplase may be considered as it appears safe, though efficacy is uncertain.

In adult AIS patients presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset or last known well who are eligible for IVT, tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) is recommended to improve functional outcomes.
In adult AIS patients presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset or last known well who are eligible for IVT, tenecteplase at a dose of 0.4 mg/kg is not recommended.
In eligible AIS patients within 6 hours of last known normal, IV urokinase is not beneficial for decreasing the odds of death or dependency.

In eligible AIS patients within 6 hours of last known normal, IV streptokinase is not recommended as it does not improve functional independence at 90 days and is associated with increased early mortality.
In AIS patients, sonothrombolysis as an adjunct to IVT is not recommended as it did not increase early neurological improvement or improve 90-day functional outcomes compared with IVT alone.

In eligible adult AIS patients with known sickle cell disease, IVT can be beneficial to improve functional outcome without increased rates of sICH, life-threatening systemic hemorrhage, or other thrombolytic complications.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1), presenting within 6 hours of symptom onset, with NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, and ASPECTS 3-10, EVT (endovascular thrombectomy) is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting 6-24 hours from symptom onset, with NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, and ASPECTS 6 or greater, EVT is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

In selected patients with AIS from anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1), presenting 6-24 hours from symptom onset, age under 80, NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, ASPECTS 3-5, and without significant mass effect on imaging, EVT is recommended to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

In selected AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting within 6 hours, age under 80, NIHSS 6 or greater, prestroke mRS 0-1, ASPECTS 0-2, and without significant mass effect, EVT is reasonable to improve functional outcomes and reduce mortality.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting within 6 hours, NIHSS 6 or greater, ASPECTS 6 or greater, and prestroke mRS of 2, EVT is reasonable to improve functional outcomes and reduce accumulated disability.

In AIS patients with anterior circulation proximal LVO (ICA or M1) presenting within 6 hours, NIHSS 6 or greater, ASPECTS 6 or greater, and prestroke mRS of 3-4, EVT might be reasonable to improve functional outcomes and reduce accumulated disability.

In AIS patients with occlusion of the dominant proximal M2 division of the MCA presenting within 6 hours, prestroke mRS 0-1, NIHSS 6 or greater, and ASPECTS 6 or greater, EVT is reasonable to improve functional outcomes, though benefits are uncertain.

In AIS patients with occlusion of the proximal nondominant or codominant M2 segment, distal MCA, anterior cerebral artery, or posterior cerebral artery, EVT is not recommended as it does not improve functional outcomes. [Current-evidence note, not part of the 2026 guideline: ORIENTAL-MeVO (NEJM 2026), published after this guideline, randomized patients with medium-vessel occlusion and NIHSS 6 or greater within 24 hours; EVT increased 90-day functional independence (58.6% vs 46.6%) but also symptomatic ICH (4.7% vs 2.2%). DISTAL, ESCAPE-MeVO and DISCOUNT found no functional benefit. This Class III grading predates ORIENTAL-MeVO.]

In AIS patients with basilar artery occlusion, baseline mRS 0-1, NIHSS 10 or greater, and PC-ASPECTS 6 or greater (mild ischemic damage), EVT within 24 hours of symptom onset is recommended to achieve better functional outcome and reduce mortality.

In AIS patients with basilar artery occlusion, baseline mRS 0-1, NIHSS 6-9, and PC-ASPECTS 6 or greater, the effectiveness of EVT within 24 hours for improving functional outcomes and reducing mortality is not well established.

In patients with minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 3 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or greater) who did not receive IVT, DAPT (aspirin plus clopidogrel with loading dose) is recommended to be initiated within 24 hours of symptom onset and continued for 21 days, followed by single antiplatelet therapy, to reduce the 90-day risk of recurrent ischemic stroke.

In patients with recent (under 24 hours) minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 5 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 6 or greater, or symptomatic intracranial/extracranial stenosis 50% or greater) who did not receive IVT, DAPT with ticagrelor (including loading dose) plus aspirin for 30 days may be considered to reduce 30-day recurrent stroke risk.

In patients with minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 5 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or greater) within 24-72 hours of onset (or NIHSS 4-5 within 24 hours) who did not receive IVT and have presumed atherosclerotic cause (50% or greater intracranial or extracranial stenosis or acute infarctions of presumed large artery origin), DAPT (clopidogrel plus aspirin) for 21 days followed by SAPT is reasonable to reduce 90-day recurrent stroke risk.

In patients with minor noncardioembolic AIS (NIHSS 3 or less) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or greater) within 24 hours of onset who did not receive IVT and carry the CYP2C19 loss-of-function allele, DAPT with ticagrelor plus aspirin for 21 days (followed by ticagrelor monotherapy) may be reasonable over clopidogrel-based DAPT to reduce 90-day recurrent stroke risk.

This is a source-inventory review, not a new clinical validation of every existing summary or supporting narrative. Existing publication-correction statuses remain separate. No separately designated ungraded consensus or good-practice recommendation set is present.

recommendations.text: A focused history, physical examination, and baseline laboratory workup (including CBC, PT/INR/PTT, creatinine/eGFR, glucose, troponin, ECG, toxicology screen, and inflammatory markers) are recommended on admission to characterize the hemorrhage type, identify active medical issues, and assess prognosis.

recommendations.section: Neuroimaging for ICH Diagnosis and Acute Course
recommendations.text: Rapid neuroimaging with CT or MRI is recommended for patients presenting with stroke-like symptoms to confirm the diagnosis of spontaneous ICH.

recommendations.section: Neuroimaging for ICH Diagnosis and Acute Course
recommendations.text: Serial head CT within the first 24 hours of symptom onset can be useful for patients with spontaneous ICH and/or IVH to evaluate for hemorrhage expansion.

recommendations.section: Neuroimaging for ICH Diagnosis and Acute Course
recommendations.text: Serial head CT can be useful for patients with spontaneous ICH and/or IVH who have a low GCS score or neurological deterioration, to evaluate for hemorrhage expansion, hydrocephalus, brain swelling, or herniation.

recommendations.section: Neuroimaging for ICH Diagnosis and Acute Course
recommendations.text: CTA within the first few hours of ICH onset may be reasonable to identify patients at risk for subsequent hemorrhage expansion.

When CTA/venography is negative in patients with spontaneous ICH, MRI and MRA are reasonable to identify a nonmacrovascular cause such as CAA, deep perforating vasculopathy, cavernous malformation, or malignancy.
Acute CTA or MRA with consideration of venography can be useful for patients with spontaneous ICH who undergo initial CT or MRI, to exclude macrovascular causes or cerebral venous thrombosis.

When initial catheter-based DSA is negative and no clear microvascular diagnosis or structural lesion is identified, a repeat DSA 3 to 6 months after ICH onset may be reasonable to detect a previously obscured vascular lesion.

For patients with spontaneous ICH requiring acute BP lowering, careful titration to achieve continuous, smooth, and sustained BP control while avoiding SBP peaks and large variability can be beneficial for functional outcomes.
Initiating acute BP treatment within 2 hours of ICH onset and reaching the target within 1 hour can be beneficial to reduce hemorrhage expansion risk and improve functional outcome.

For patients with mild to moderate spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP 150-220 mm Hg, acutely lowering SBP to a target of 140 mm Hg (maintaining 130-150 mm Hg range) is safe and may be reasonable for improving functional outcomes.
The safety and efficacy of intensive BP lowering are not well established for patients with large or severe spontaneous ICH or those requiring surgical decompression.
Acute lowering of SBP to <130 mm Hg is potentially harmful in patients with mild to moderate spontaneous ICH presenting with SBP >150 mm Hg.
Immediate discontinuation of anticoagulation and rapid reversal are recommended as soon as possible after diagnosis of anticoagulant-associated spontaneous ICH to improve survival.
4-factor PCC is recommended over FFP for patients with VKA-associated spontaneous ICH and INR >= 2.0 to achieve rapid INR correction and limit hemorrhage expansion.
Intravenous vitamin K is recommended immediately after coagulation factor replacement (PCC or other) for VKA-associated spontaneous ICH to prevent subsequent INR elevation and hemorrhage expansion.
PCC may be reasonable for patients with VKA-associated spontaneous ICH and INR 1.3-1.9 to achieve rapid INR correction and limit hemorrhage expansion.
Andexanet alfa is reasonable for patients with direct factor Xa inhibitor-associated spontaneous ICH to reverse the anticoagulant effect.
recommendations.currentEvidenceNote: US safety and availability update reviewed 2026-09-26 (not part of the 2022 guideline): FDA concluded that the serious risks of Andexxa outweigh its benefits; US commercial sales ended on 22 December 2025. In ANNEXA-I (2024), andexanet improved hemostatic efficacy versus usual care (67.0% vs 53.1%) but increased thrombotic events (10.3% vs 5.6%), including ischemic stroke (6.5% vs 1.5%), with no appreciable difference in mRS or 30-day death. The 2026 NCS/SCCM focused update conditionally recommends 4F-PCC over andexanet; in the US, 4F-PCC or aPCC (off-label for this indication) is now the principal reversal option for factor Xa inhibitor-associated ICH. This 2022 statement keeps its original grading and is not a current US endorsement or evidence of andexanet availability.

Connolly et al., N Engl J Med 2024 (ANNEXA-I)

recommendations.text: Idarucizumab is reasonable for patients with dabigatran-associated spontaneous ICH to reverse the anticoagulant effect.
4-factor PCC or activated PCC (aPCC) may be considered for patients with direct factor Xa inhibitor-associated spontaneous ICH to improve hemostasis.

Activated charcoal may be reasonable for patients with dabigatran- or factor Xa inhibitor-associated spontaneous ICH when the DOAC was ingested within the previous few hours, to prevent further drug absorption.
When idarucizumab is unavailable, aPCC or PCCs may be considered for patients with dabigatran-associated spontaneous ICH to improve hemostasis.
When idarucizumab is unavailable, renal replacement therapy may be considered for patients with dabigatran-associated spontaneous ICH to reduce circulating dabigatran concentration.
Intravenous protamine is reasonable for patients with UFH-associated spontaneous ICH to reverse the anticoagulant effect of heparin.
Intravenous protamine may be considered for patients with LMWH-associated spontaneous ICH to partially reverse the anticoagulant effect.
Platelet transfusion might be considered for patients with aspirin-associated spontaneous ICH who require emergency neurosurgery, to reduce postoperative bleeding and mortality.
The effectiveness of desmopressin, with or without platelet transfusions, to reduce hematoma expansion in patients with antiplatelet-associated spontaneous ICH is uncertain.
Frequent neurological assessments (including GCS) by ED nurses are recommended during the early hyperacute phase of spontaneous ICH to detect changes in neurological status or level of consciousness.

For patients with cerebellar ICH who are deteriorating neurologically, have brainstem compression and/or hydrocephalus from ventricular obstruction, or have cerebellar ICH volume >=15 mL, immediate surgical removal of the hemorrhage with or without EVD is recommended in preference to medical management alone to reduce mortality.
recommendations.localNote: Local operational note (June 2026 institutional overlay — NOT AHA/ASA guideline content): the local June 2026 initial-evaluation algorithm does not use cerebellar hematoma volume alone as an operative trigger.

recommendations.text: A baseline hemorrhage severity score is recommended as part of the initial evaluation for patients with spontaneous ICH to provide an overall measure of clinical severity.
A baseline severity score might be reasonable as a general framework for communication with patients and their caregivers about prognosis.
A baseline severity score alone is not recommended as the sole basis for forecasting individual prognosis or deciding to limit life-sustaining treatment in patients with spontaneous ICH.

recommendations.section: Clinical variables as predictors of functional outcome — PICO 2: Admission NIHSS
recommendations.classNote: Against (suggests the predictor NOT be relied upon)
recommendations.text: When counseling critically ill adults with AIS or their surrogates, we suggest the admission National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) alone not be considered a reliable predictor of poor functional outcome assessed at 3 months or later (weak recommendation; very low quality evidence).

recommendations.section: Clinical prediction models as predictors of functional outcome — PICO 10: ASTRAL score
recommendations.classNote: Against (suggests the model NOT be relied upon)
recommendations.text: When counseling critically ill patients with AIS or their surrogates, we suggest the Acute Stroke Registry and Analysis of Lausanne (ASTRAL) score not be considered a reliable predictor of poor functional outcome assessed at 3 months or later (weak recommendation; low quality evidence). guidelines.title: Treatment of Antithrombotic-Associated Intracranial Hemorrhage in Adults: A Focused Guideline Update from the Neurocritical Care Society and the Society of Critical Care Medicine

recommendations.section: Recommendation 1-1 — Spontaneous FXa ICH: PCC preferred to andexanet
recommendations.text: We suggest using 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate rather than andexanet alfa in patients with factor Xa inhibitor-associated spontaneous ICH (conditional recommendation; moderate certainty evidence).

recommendations.section: Recommendation 1-2 — Traumatic FXa ICH: PCC preferred to andexanet
recommendations.text: We suggest using 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate rather than andexanet alfa in patients with factor Xa inhibitor-associated traumatic ICH (conditional recommendation; very low certainty evidence).

recommendations.section: Recommendation 2-1 — Spontaneous IPH, antiplatelets, no surgery: avoid platelets
recommendations.text: we suggest against administering platelet transfusions to patients with spontaneous intraparenchymal hemorrhage taking antiplatelet agents who do not require neurosurgical intervention. (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence).

recommendations.section: Recommendation 2-2 — Spontaneous IPH, aspirin, surgery: give platelets
recommendations.text: we suggest administering platelet transfusions to patients with spontaneous intraparenchymal hemorrhage who were on aspirin therapy who require neurosurgical intervention (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty evidence).

recommendations.section: Recommendation 2-3 — Traumatic ICH, antiplatelets: no recommendation
recommendations.text: we make no recommendation regarding administration of platelets for patients with traumatic intracranial hemorrhage who were on antiplatelet therapy.

recommendations.section: Recommendation 3-1 — Antiplatelet-associated ICH, DDAVP: no recommendation
recommendations.text: we make no recommendation regarding use of desmopressin in patients with intracranial hemorrhage on antiplatelet therapy.

recommendations.section: Recommendation 4-1 — Small IPH, anticoagulant reversal: no recommendation
recommendations.text: we cannot make a recommendation regarding treatment of anticoagulant effects in patients with small intraparenchymal hemorrhage due to lack of evidence.

recommendations.section: Recommendation 5-1 — Traumatic ICH: viscoelastic-assay-guided treatment if available
recommendations.text: we suggest using VHA-guided management in patients with traumatic intracranial hemorrhage, when VHAs are available (conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence).

recommendations.text: In patients with recent stroke or TIA (within 30 days) attributable to severe intracranial stenosis (70-99%), adding clopidogrel 75 mg/d to aspirin for up to 90 days is reasonable to further reduce recurrent stroke risk.

For noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA, aspirin 50-325 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, or aspirin 25 mg plus extended-release dipyridamole 200 mg twice daily is recommended for secondary prevention.

For recent minor noncardioembolic ischemic stroke (NIHSS 3 or below) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 4 or above), dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) is recommended to be initiated early (ideally within 12-24 hours, at least within 7 days of onset) and continued for 21 to 90 days, followed by single antiplatelet therapy, to reduce recurrent ischemic stroke.

For recent (within 24 hours) minor to moderate stroke (NIHSS 5 or below), high-risk TIA (ABCD2 6 or above), or symptomatic 30% or greater stenosis of a relevant artery, dual antiplatelet therapy with ticagrelor plus aspirin for 30 days may be considered to reduce 30-day recurrent stroke but may increase serious bleeding risk including ICH.

Continuous dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) beyond 90 days or use of triple antiplatelet therapy is associated with excess hemorrhage risk in noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA patients.

guidelines.title: SVIN 2025 Guideline: EVT for Large Infarct

recommendations.text: In patients with anterior circulation stroke presenting within 0-6 h from symptom onset, baseline mRS score 0-1, age 18-80 years, occlusion of the ICA or MCA M1 segment, and ASPECTS of 0-5 on noncontrast CT or MRI, EVT is recommended. (Evidence: LASTE trial; meta-analyses AlMajali et al, Roman et al, Winkelmeier et al)

In patients with anterior circulation LVO presenting within 6-24 h from symptom onset, baseline mRS score 0-1, age 18-80 years, occlusion of the ICA or MCA M1 segment, and ASPECTS of 3-5 on noncontrast CT or MRI, EVT is recommended. (Evidence: ANGEL-ASPECT, RESCUE-Japan LIMIT; meta-analyses Palaiodimou et al, Wei et al, Li et al)

In patients with anterior circulation LVO presenting within 6-24 h from symptom onset, baseline mRS score 0-1, age 18-80 years, occlusion of the ICA or MCA M1 segment with CTP imaging according to the SELECT2 and ANGEL-ASPECT eligibility criteria, EVT is recommended. (Evidence: ANGEL-ASPECT, SELECT2)

In patients with anterior circulation LVO presenting within 6-24 h from symptom onset, baseline mRS score 0-1, age 18-80 years, occlusion of the ICA or MCA M1 segment, and ASPECTS of 0-2 on noncontrast CT or MRI, the benefit of EVT is uncertain.
